policy: These are promoted scientific claims. Numeric claims are included only where the full text was reviewed and the locator names the supporting section, page, table, figure, or equation. Legacy abstract-only numbers are deliberately absent.

claims.claimText: In FP-Agent's released closed-set evaluation, behavioral interaction features separate the studied actors more effectively than browser metadata, while held-out-task results show a generalization loss.
claims.claimBoundary: This does not establish unseen-agent-family generalization; the local project has only used the released split and model.

claims.claimText: The FP-Agent artifact supports released-split review, but reproducing that result is not equivalent to retraining or validating on an unseen executor family.
claims.claimBoundary: Keep released-split reproduction, new-family evaluation, and matched human collection as separate evidence levels.

claims.claimText: UI trajectories can attribute known browser-agent implementations, but the paper assumes automation is already known and reports task/site dependence.
claims.claimBoundary: Agent-family attribution is not the same problem as human-versus-agent detection.

claims.claimText: Under the paper's selected three-failure threshold, the six-item active challenge detected 97.1% of 526 deployed agents while flagging 4.1% of 1,007 presumed humans.

locator.section: Prolific Method and Results; Human Validation; Practical Recommendations

claims.claimBoundary: This is an active survey intervention with platform-verified human labels, not passive mouse/keyboard trace detection.

claims.claimText: WebCloak disrupts parse-then-interpret scraping through structural and semantic defenses; successful disruption does not identify the actor that initiated a session.
claims.claimBoundary: Treat it as executor/threat characterization and active defense, not a passive detector benchmark.

claims.claimText: When feature definitions, repetitions, outlier handling, attempt counts, and threshold rules were fixed on one dataset, the three strongest compared keystroke detectors fell within a narrow 9.6%-10.2% equal-error-rate band.
claims.claimBoundary: The absolute error rates belong to a fixed-password, single-machine protocol; the transferable result is the need to pin the evaluation contract.

claims.claimText: Mouse-dynamics results can reflect pointing-device and computing-environment differences rather than stable identity behavior when those variables are not controlled across enrollment and verification.
claims.claimBoundary: Executor, browser, device, viewport, and task provenance must therefore stay available for confound audits.

claims.claimText: Authentication practicality depends on the amount and duration of mouse activity required before a decision, not only on an aggregate error rate.
claims.claimBoundary: The detector report should pair discrimination metrics with horizon and abstention coverage.

claims.claimText: Keystroke dynamics models habitual typing rhythm using inter-key latencies and key durations rather than the semantic content of the typed string.
claims.claimBoundary: Identity verification is not the same label problem as human-versus-agent detection, so feature definitions transfer more directly than reported accuracy.

claims.claimText: The human/bot/cyborg formulation is an early demonstration that a mixed human-automation actor cannot be represented faithfully by a binary human-or-bot label.
claims.claimBoundary: Its signals are account- and post-level; they do not transfer directly to mouse/keyboard event features.

claims.claimText: BeCAPTCHA-Mouse grounds synthetic cursor generation in a neuromotor/lognormal trajectory model and evaluates detectors against generated mouse paths.
claims.claimBoundary: The negative class is a trajectory generator, not an LLM agent completing matched browser tasks.

claims.claimText: Workflow-guided exploration constrains web-interface reinforcement learning with demonstration-derived workflows and evaluates both benchmark and live-web task variants.
claims.claimBoundary: It supplies agent/environment context, not human-versus-agent labels or passive event traces.

claims.claimText: The controlled corpus combines more than 14,000 CaptchaSolve30k human sessions, 5,000 simulated bot samples, and 1,025 Claude/Playwright agent sessions across 10 tasks.
claims.claimBoundary: Only the human and agent classes are real interaction data; the bot class is generated from specified distributions.

claims.claimText: Each agent session is recorded as JSONL containing mousemove, mousedown, mouseup, click, keydown, keyup, and scroll events with timestamps and isTrusted.

locator.appendix: Appendix A: Event Parsing, Button State Machine, and Trajectory Segmentation

claims.claimBoundary: The public-release paragraph does not yet provide a verified artifact URL for these session files.

claims.claimText: Human sessions come from CAPTCHA solving, whereas agent sessions come from ten different browser tasks; the task-domain analysis is an ablation, not a matched-task human collection.
claims.claimBoundary: The paper cannot establish task-invariant human-versus-agent separation under a fully matched interaction protocol.

claims.claimText: The discriminative signal is attributed to Playwright's event-emission pattern, especially missing raw pointer and wheel streams, rather than to agent reasoning.

locator.section: Section 4.1; Section 12, What We Are Actually Detecting

claims.claimBoundary: A detector trained on this signature should be described as executor-sensitive until tested on independent OS-level and API-level executors.

claims.claimText: In the paper's controlled benchmark, mouse_event_rate plus teleport_click_ratio produced 100% observed agent recall across the tested evasion levels with 0.994 agent precision; the paper also shows the single-feature regime can collapse into an always-agent classifier.
claims.claimBoundary: These are in-corpus observations under the paper's task/executor design, not a universal minimal detector.

claims.claimText: The evaluated threat model covers API-driven browser automation and does not test OS-level input simulation such as PyAutoGUI.
claims.claimBoundary: Claims should not be extended to hardware-event injection or arbitrary desktop automation.

claims.claimText: The paper states that code, trained models, processed datasets, feature extraction, and evaluation scripts will be released upon publication, but no public artifact URL was verified on 2026-08-11.
claims.claimBoundary: Do not describe the data or code as currently released; recheck the paper record before planning a reproduction.
